chunks: Die vs wafer vs package. The question: What is the difference between the die, wafer, and package?
A wafer is a thin round disc of silicon on which hundreds of copies of a circuit are built at the same time. Each copy, once cut out, is called a die.
A package is the case around a die: it protects the die and gives it connections you can solder to a board. They are the same silicon at three stages.
Think of baking cookies. The wafer is the whole sheet of dough. The dies are the individual cookies you cut from it. The package is the box each cookie goes in for shipping.
Cookies with a burnt spot get thrown away, and a bigger cookie is more likely to catch a burnt spot. Also, fewer big cookies fit on the sheet.
That is why chip cost depends so strongly on die size.
The wafer is the batch unit; the die is the functional unit; the package is the product unit.
Two test stages catch different faults: wafer sort stops bad dies from being packaged, final test catches assembly and packaging damage and bins parts by speed.
Wafer: the silicon disc, usually 300 mm across for modern chips. Die: one rectangular copy of the circuit, cut from the wafer. Package: the case and connections around the die.
Wafer sort: testing each die on the wafer before it is cut, so bad ones are not packaged. Yield: the share of dies that work.
A 300 mm wafer has an area of about 70,700 mm². Suppose each die is 100 mm². Dividing gives about 707, but dies at the curved edge do not fit, so you get about 640 whole dies.
Now make the die eight times bigger, 800 mm². Dividing gives about 88, and after edge losses about 65 dies. So an 8 times bigger die gives about 10 times fewer dies.
Add the fact that a bigger die is more likely to contain a flaw, and a big die costs far more than 8 times as much. That is the whole idea.
"A wafer is a thin disc of silicon, usually 300 millimetres, on which hundreds of identical circuits are fabricated at once. Each rectangular copy is a die.
The wafer is tested, cut into dies, and the good dies are mounted in packages, which connect the tiny die pads to board-scale balls or leads, protect the silicon, remove heat and make it solderable.
Dies per wafer is roughly wafer area over die area minus edge loss, so a bigger die costs disproportionately more."
